summaries.gardner: Union Pacific is a 160-year-old incumbent in a mature, slow-growing industry, so it fails most Rule Breaker traits such as leading an emerging industry or being called overvalued for its growth. Its strengths are a durable competitive position and good management execution, which are more Rule Maker than Rule Breaker qualities.
summaries.buffett: UNP fits much of Buffett's approach: a simple, essential business with a durable moat (a western rail duopoly with BNSF, which Berkshire itself owns), 127 consecutive years of dividends and EPS that more than doubled from $5.49 in 2015 to $11.98 in 2025. The drawbacks are heavy capital needs, about $30.3B of debt and a full price of about 23 times trailing earnings, offering little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the irreplaceable rights-of-way and the rational two-player western market, which make permanent failure very unlikely. He might worry about capital intensity, regulation and union-heavy labour, and the $85B Norfolk Southern acquisition adds integration and regulatory risk to an otherwise simple 'great business at a fair price' case.
summaries.lynch: In Lynch's terms UNP is a stalwart: a large, steady company with high-single-digit EPS growth guided for 2026 and a 2% dividend yield. At about 23 times trailing and 21 times forward earnings against roughly 8% EPS growth, the PEG is well above 1, so it is not a Lynch bargain.
summaries.fisher: Fisher would credit UNP's strong operating management (59.8% operating ratio in 2025, record service metrics) and long-term plans such as a transcontinental network. But it has little R&D or new-product development and modest revenue growth, so it fits Fisher's emphasis on growth through innovation only partly.
summaries.graham: UNP meets Graham's size, long dividend record (127 years) and ten-year earnings growth tests, and has been profitable every year. It clearly fails his price tests: about 23 times trailing earnings and about 8 times book value, with a current ratio just under 1.
summaries.thiel: Union Pacific is a quasi-monopoly by geography rather than by technology: its network and durable position are strong but it has no proprietary technology that is ten times better. It scores well on distribution and durability but poorly on technology, secret insight and timing questions in Zero to One.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth at a reasonable price, ideally tied to big technology shifts; UNP offers durability and strong cash flow but low revenue growth and no AI exposure. The Norfolk Southern deal is a possible catalyst, but the setup is a defensive compounder rather than a high-growth idea.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on what will change over the next 18-24 months: UNP's possible catalysts are the STB ruling on the Norfolk Southern merger (final briefs due May 28, 2027) and an industrial recovery. Earnings estimates have edged up but are not accelerating sharply, so it is unlikely to be a high-conviction concentrated bet.
summaries.smith: UNP passes Terry Smith's 'good company' tests on high operating margins (about 40%), resilience and strong cash generation, but it is capital intensive and relies on debt rather than producing high returns on unleveraged capital. At about 32 times free cash flow it is not cheap, so it fits the 'don't overpay' rule only partly.
summaries.greenblatt: UNP earns a solid return on capital, but its earnings yield (operating income of $9,846M against an enterprise value of about $200B, roughly 4.9%) is low. It would not rank highly on the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: Akre's stool asks for an extraordinary business, skilled and honest management, and good reinvestment opportunities. UNP has a great business and capable management, but reinvestment is limited to maintaining and modestly expanding its network, so most cash goes to dividends and buybacks; the third leg is weak.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses in temporary distress bought at deep discounts with low downside. UNP is simple and has low permanent-loss risk, but it is not distressed or cheap at about 23 times earnings, so it is not a Dhandho bet.
summaries.wood: UNP is not a disruptive-innovation company and has no exposure to ARK's platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or sequencing). Autonomous trucking, one of ARK's themes, is more a threat to it than an opportunity, so it does not fit Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: UNP closely resembles businesses Ackman likes: simple, predictable, free-cash-flow generative, with high barriers to entry (he previously ran an activist campaign at Canadian Pacific). Its debt, regulatory exposure and full valuation reduce the appeal, and the merger adds event risk.
summaries.sleep: Sleep favoured businesses that share scale savings with customers to grow stronger over time. UNP's efficiency gains have mainly gone to shareholders through higher margins rather than lower prices, although the Norfolk Southern merger is pitched as saving shippers about $3.5 billion a year; it fits only partly.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for start-ups attacking huge new markets with great technology; Union Pacific is a mature incumbent. It solves a large, important problem (moving heavy freight cheaply) but has none of the venture-style traits Sequoia sought.
summaries.nash: UNP passes Nash's zone and profitability tests (large cap, about 40% operating margin, profitable) but fails his instant-kill screens on debt exceeding cash and revenue growth below 10%. Valuation checks (DCF at a 12% discount rate and PEG) also point to a full price, so it scores poorly overall.

momentum.evidence: The stock closed at $289.04 on Oct 16, 2026, near the top of its 52-week range of $215.53-$315.99, with StockAnalysis showing market value up about 28%, though whether it beat the market over the same period is not confirmed.

g4.evidence: CEO Jim Vena is a respected 40-plus-year railroader who delivered record 2025 results, but the company has no famous anchor investor or partner beyond broad institutional ownership.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly see UNP as fairly valued: the average price target was $327.63 versus a $289.04 price in October 2026, and it is not commonly called overvalued.

simple.evidence: It owns tracks and trains and charges customers to move freight across 23 western states, a business any careful generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: It has paid dividends for 127 consecutive years and diluted EPS rose from $5.49 in 2015 to $11.98 in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Reporting is clear and capital allocation has been shareholder-focused (dividends of $3,236M and buybacks of $2,679M in 2025), but critics question the $2.5 billion break fee and regulatory risk accepted in the Norfolk Southern deal.

b6.evidence: Management stuck to its core railroad for years, but the proposed roughly $85B Norfolk Southern acquisition is a large empire-expanding bet, even if strategically argued.

roic.evidence: After-tax operating income of roughly $7.7B on about $49B of debt plus equity less cash implies a mid-teens return, but it relies on $30.3B of debt and equity of only $20.7B.

fcf.evidence: In 2025 operating cash flow of $9,290M less capital investments of $3,791M left $5,499M of free cash flow, about 77% of $7,138M net income.

b10.evidence: It pays out most of its profit through dividends and buybacks, and the retained portion has mainly sustained the network, while revenue rose only from $24,875M in 2022 to $24,510M in 2025.

safety.evidence: At about 23 times trailing EPS of $12.35 and roughly 32 times 2025 free cash flow, the price is not well below a conservative value estimate.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 21 for a top-quality railroad guiding high-single-digit EPS growth is full but not extreme.

mu5.evidence: Its irreplaceable 32,889-mile network, duopoly position and essential role in moving U.S. goods leave few ways for the business to fail; the main risks are regulation, accidents and the merger.

reinvest.evidence: It reinvests about $3.3-3.8B a year in capital spending to keep the network efficient, but growth opportunities at high incremental returns are limited outside the Norfolk Southern deal.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic stalwart: a large, steady company guiding high-single-digit EPS growth with a clear story of efficiency gains and, possibly, a transcontinental merger.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 23.4 is well above its expected high-single-digit EPS growth rate.

runway.evidence: Organic revenue growth is low (+1.1% in 2025), with growth depending on truck-to-rail conversion, Mexico trade and the proposed Norfolk Southern combination.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell from 679.1M in 2020 to 594.0M in Q2 2026, but there is no evidence of notable insider open-market buying.

ly8.evidence: Although railroading is 'boring', UNP is a $172B company covered by more than 20 analysts and widely owned.

fi2.evidence: It develops new service offerings (such as premium intermodal and Mexico services) and pursues the transcontinental merger, but rail is a mature service with little new-product development.

fi3.evidence: Union Pacific does not report a separate R&D figure, so the payoff from technology spending cannot be measured.

fi4.evidence: It achieves core pricing gains above inflation and added 113,000 carloads in 2025, but its sales success comes largely from network position rather than unusual selling skill.

longterm.evidence: The Norfolk Southern merger shows long-term ambition, but management also targets near-term operating-ratio and EPS goals (high-single to low-double-digit EPS CAGR through 2027).

gr1.evidence: It is the largest U.S. railroad by revenue ($24,510M in 2025) with a market value of about $172B.

ni10.evidence: It has been profitable every year of the last decade, with net income of $5,349M in 2020 rising to $7,138M in 2025.

gr4.evidence: The company says it has paid dividends on its common stock for 127 consecutive years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $5.49 in 2015 to $11.98 in 2025, more than doubling.

gr6.evidence: The price of $289.04 is about 26 times average 2023-2025 diluted EPS of about $11.17.

gr7.evidence: With a P/E of about 23.4 and price-to-book of about 8.3 (equity $20,673M, 594M shares), the product is roughly 194, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Rail technology is shared across the industry; its advantage is network geography, not proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Nearshoring to Mexico and freight shifting from trucks could help, but freight volumes are only growing slowly (carloads +2% in Q2 2026).

th3.evidence: It started as one of the original transcontinental railroads in a large market rather than dominating a small niche and expanding.

team.evidence: Management under Jim Vena is highly capable operationally, but it is not a founder-led or world-renowned team.

th5.evidence: Its network itself is the distribution: about 10,000 customers sit directly on or connect to its lines, ports and six Mexico gateways.

durable.evidence: Rights-of-way that cannot be rebuilt and a two-railroad western market should hold for 10-20 years, though autonomous trucks are a long-term risk.

th7.evidence: The plan for the first U.S. transcontinental railroad via Norfolk Southern is a bold opportunity, but it is widely known and opposed by rivals and shippers.

trend.evidence: Rail benefits mildly from nearshoring and decarbonisation of freight, but it is not a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift like AI or cloud.

dr1.evidence: After Q2 2026 (adjusted EPS $3.41 vs $3.20 consensus) management raised its 2026 EPS growth outlook to high single digits, but growth is steady rather than accelerating sharply.

dr2.evidence: Progress through STB merger review and continued efficiency gains could improve the outlook, but the outcome is uncertain and largely known to the market.

dr4.evidence: As a cyclical, debt-funded business it benefits from lower rates and a stronger industrial economy, but management calls the economic outlook mixed.

dr6.evidence: STB milestones on the Norfolk Southern merger (comments due Nov 18, 2026, final briefs May 28, 2027) and quarterly results could move the stock.

dr7.evidence: Low growth, merger uncertainty and a full valuation make it unlikely to merit a large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Railroads do not report gross margin, but its operating margin of about 40% in 2025 is among the highest of any transport company and signals pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: 2025 free cash flow of $5,499M against a $171.7B market value is a yield of about 3.2%, reasonable but not cheap for a low-growth business.

gb2.evidence: 2025 operating income of $9,846M is only about 4.9% of an enterprise value of roughly $200B.

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback: 2025 was a record year for its operating ratio and Q2 2026 revenue rose 12%.

pa4.evidence: With essential, irreplaceable infrastructure and consistent profits for decades, the chance of permanent capital loss in the business is small, though overpaying is possible.

wo1.evidence: Union Pacific is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Rail unit costs fall only slowly through efficiency, not the steep cost declines that unlock large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It is a single-platform freight railroad with no combination of innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market of North American freight will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Fuel surcharges pass most fuel cost changes to customers, but volumes depend on the economy, coal and grain markets, and it carries $30.3B of debt.

ns1.evidence: Efficiency gains have largely gone into margins (operating ratio 59.8%) and shareholder returns, while core prices rise above inflation; only the merger pitch promises about $3.5 billion in shipper savings.

ns4.evidence: If the Norfolk Southern merger is approved it could be stronger as the only coast-to-coast railroad, but without it its position is similar to today's.

va2.evidence: It solves the large problem of moving heavy goods like grain, chemicals and cars across long distances cheaply.

tn1.evidence: It is an old freight railroad, not a company built for a new secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a mature regional railroad, while the Norfolk Southern merger could turn it into the first U.S. transcontinental carrier, though this is well publicised.

tn3.evidence: It is a $172B U.S. large cap, not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue grew in 2024, 2025 and H1 2026 and it is highly profitable, but debt of $30,327M far exceeds cash of $2,114M, a typical feature of infrastructure owners.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive, but debt ($30,327M) has far exceeded cash and short-term investments ($2,114M) in every recent quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 1.1% in 2025 and 7.4% in H1 2026, below 10%.

tn7.evidence: 2025 revenue growth of 1.1% plus a free-cash-flow margin of about 22.4% is roughly 23.5, below 40.

tn8.evidence: In 2025 revenue (+1.1%) grew slightly faster than operating expenses (+0.9%), but in H1 2026 operating expenses (+7.9%) outpaced revenue (+7.4%).

tn9.evidence: It trips instant kills: debt of $30,327M exceeds cash of $2,114M and revenue growth is well below 10%.

tn10.evidence: The Norfolk Southern merger faces a full STB review with opposition from BNSF and shippers, and railroads face ongoing safety and access regulation.

tn11.evidence: It provides rail freight transport that helps shippers move heavy goods long distances cheaply, and charges per-shipment rates plus fuel surcharges; customers choose it because it reaches their facilities at lower cost than trucks.

tn18.evidence: Jim Vena has a strong execution record (record 2025 operating ratio and EPS), but he has been CEO only since 2023, is not a founder and no notable open-market purchases are known.

tn20.evidence: It beat Q2 2026 estimates (adjusted EPS $3.41 vs $3.20 consensus, revenue $6.86B vs $6.65B), but a consistent multi-quarter beat record was not verified.

tn21.evidence: No fraud, auditor change or clown CEO, but the very large Norfolk Southern acquisition and flat operating margins are flags under Nash's list.

tn22.evidence: It has $24.5B of revenue, strong profits, a shrinking share count and no hype-driven share sales.

tn24.evidence: At about 32 times free cash flow the price implies faster sustained growth than the roughly 1% revenue growth and high-single-digit EPS growth it is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using about -0.5% three-year average revenue growth and a 22% FCF margin, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth give an equity value of roughly $31B (about $52 per share), far below the $289 price.
